analysis.one_liner: Creates a federal extreme-heat warning system and funds community cooling projects.
analysis.headline: A Senate bill to coordinate federal action on dangerous heat, backed by 10 senators, has sat in the Commerce Committee without a hearing since August 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would stand up a permanent federal system inside NOAA to track, warn about, and plan for dangerous heat, coordinated across more than a dozen agencies including CDC, FEMA, OSHA, and the Weather Service. It would commission a National Academies study on gaps in heat response, including which federal heat tools were discontinued, and create a grant program for projects like cooling centers, cool roofs, urban trees, and workplace heat policies, with at least 40% of grant money going to low-income communities and communities of color that bear the worst heat. It authorizes about $201.5 million over five years.
analysis.who_benefits: Outdoor workers such as farm and construction laborers, older adults, pregnant people, young children, people with disabilities, people experiencing homelessness, and residents of low-income urban neighborhoods that trap heat. Tribal communities and rural areas with few heat resources also gain. The bill directs at least 40% of grant funds to communities with environmental justice concerns or low incomes.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Outdoor workers, the elderly, low-income city neighborhoods

how_it_helps.text: Heat has been the leading cause of weather-related death in the United States over the last 30 years and drives more than 65,000 emergency room visits a year, yet few communities have sufficient heat-health information and resources, according to the bill's findings. [S2]

The bill would create a permanent National Integrated Heat Health Information System within NOAA, run by an interagency committee spanning NOAA, CDC, FEMA, OSHA, the Department of Labor, and other agencies, to coordinate warnings, planning, and response across all levels of government. [S2]

It would create a community heat resilience grant program funding cooling centers, cool roofs and pavements, urban tree planting, building retrofits for cooling, grid resilience for air conditioning, and local heat emergency plans, prioritizing communities with the greatest heat disparities by race, ethnicity, or income. [S2]

The bill would require a National Academies study identifying gaps in heat data and response, including how many schools, prisons, and public facilities lack air conditioning, and how the discontinuation of federal heat-health tools has changed heat risk and data collection. [S2]

analysis.who_pays: General federal taxpayers. The bill authorizes $20 million a year for the NOAA system and committee, $500,000 a year for three years for the study, and $10-30 million a year for the grant program — about $201.5 million over five years. Because these are authorizations, Congress would still have to approve the money in annual spending bills.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers, about $201.5 million over five years

drawbacks.text: The roughly $201.5 million authorized over five years is a new federal spending commitment, and authorizations do not guarantee funding — Congress would have to appropriate the money each year or the programs would not materialize. [S2]

The bill does not set any federal workplace heat standard; it funds training and support for local workplace heat policies, so it coordinates and studies the problem rather than directly mandating protections for workers, who face the highest heat risk. [S2]

Grant funding is discretionary — the Director 'may' establish the program — and an interagency committee spanning 16-plus agencies risks duplicating existing emergency-management and public-health programs if coordination falls short. [S2]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The cost is small relative to federal budgets, and the bill targets spending at the populations that die in heat waves — outdoor workers, older adults, and low-income urban neighborhoods. Its limits are real: no federal heat standard for workers, funding is authorized but not guaranteed, and much of the bill is coordination and study rather than direct protection. Still, for the price, it addresses a hazard that kills more Americans than any other weather event.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee in August 2025, and it has stayed there — no hearing, no markup, no vote, while the current Congress continues.

narrative.text: Senator Edward Markey introduced the bill on August 1, 2025, joined by nine cosponsors — eight Democrats and one Independent. [S1][S4]
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation, and the public record shows no further action since. [S4]

The bill would authorize about $201.5 million over fiscal years 2026 through 2030, including $100 million for community heat resilience grants and $100 million for the NOAA heat-health system and interagency committee. [S2]

The grant program would require that at least 40% of assistance each year go to communities with environmental justice concerns or low-income communities, prioritizing areas with heat disparities tied to race, ethnicity, or income. [S2]
The bill's findings note that extreme heat has been the leading cause of weather-related death in the U.S. for 30 years and causes more than 65,000 emergency room visits annually. [S2]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far nobody has gained or lost — the bill simply has not moved, and the gap in federal heat coordination and funding it would fill remains open.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: So far, nobody — it just sits in committee

for.name: Sen. Edward Markey
for.role: U.S. Senator from Massachusetts; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on August 1, 2025 and became its lead sponsor in the Senate.

for.name: Sens. Padilla, Gallego, Heinrich, Blumenthal, Merkley, Wyden, Duckworth, Booker, and Sanders
for.what_they_did: Signed on as original cosponsors when the bill was introduced; none is on the committee holding the bill.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Ted Cruz (R-TX)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral in August 2025 and has taken no action on it since — no hearing, no markup, no vote scheduled.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.role: Controls the Senate floor calendar in the 119th Congress
against.what_they_did: Has not brought the bill to the floor; with no Republican cosponsors, it has no path to a floor vote without committee action.

sides.party_line_note: All 10 supporters are Democrats or the independent who caucuses with Democrats; no Republican senator has cosponsored, and the bill sits in a Republican-chaired committee.

industries.note: Grant-funded projects for air conditioning upgrades, cool roofs, building retrofits, and grid resilience would direct public money toward these industries' services. The spending serves the same communities the industry serves, so its interest runs alongside residents'.

The bill imposes no federal heat standard on employers, but it funds training and support for local workplace heat policies, which could lead to stricter local rules over time. In the near term it changes little for them.

analysis.trajectory: With no Republican cosponsors, no committee hearing since the August 2025 referral, and the Commerce Committee controlled by the other party, the bill is likely to die quietly when this Congress ends in January 2027 — the typical fate for a first-term bill of this size unless a committee chair takes it up.
